clue.text: Incredibly changeable people used to be footballers

parts.note: used to be is the past tense were
Wolves is the nickname of Wolverhampton Wanderers, an English football club

explanation.surface: Some former footballers have, astonishingly, become fickle characters.
explanation.walkthrough: WOLVES is Wolverhampton Wanderers, an English football club. 'Incredibly' belongs to the definition: these shape-shifters are literally beyond belief.
explanation.definitionFit: Lycanthropes of legend transform from human to beast, so they are people capable of an unbelievable change.

clue.text: Group of women needing exercise — there's the rub

parts.note: WI is the Women's Institute, a British organisation of women's groups
PE is physical education, exercise at school

explanation.surface: Women's group need to exercise; that's the difficulty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'there's the rub' is a Hamlet quotation meaning a snag, but here 'rub' is just a verb meaning wipe. WI, the Women's Institute, is a British club for women.
explanation.definitionFit: To wipe a surface is to rub it clean.

clue.text: Engineers can use odd bits for train

parts.note: RE is the Royal Engineers, a British Army corps
a can is a tin

indicators.note: the odd bits are the first and third letters of the word

explanation.surface: Engineers can make use of spare parts for a railway train.
explanation.walkthrough: 'train' is not a railway: it is a group of followers.
explanation.definitionFit: A retinue is the train of attendants following an important person.

clue.text: Reputable source contemplated

parts.note: a well is a source of water
to have thought of something is to have contemplated it

explanation.surface: A trustworthy source was considered.
explanation.walkthrough: 'source' sounds like an informant, but it is a water source.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone highly regarded by others is reputable, of good repute.

clue.text: English critic is seen after sabbatical, mostly

indicators.note: seen after means placed following the other piece
mostly means all but the last letter

parts.note: a sabbatical is a period of leave

explanation.surface: An English critic has been noticed after most of a sabbatical.
explanation.walkthrough: F. R. Leavis was an influential Cambridge literary critic.
explanation.definitionFit: F. R. Leavis was a twentieth-century English literary critic.

clue.text: Abstained from having key cut

parts.note: Esc is the escape key on a keyboard
to hew is to cut, especially with an axe

explanation.surface: Someone avoided having a key cut.
explanation.walkthrough: 'key cut' suggests a locksmith, but the key is on a computer keyboard.
explanation.definitionFit: To eschew something is to deliberately avoid or abstain from it.

clue.text: Bag for member of camera crew

definitions.meaning: to bag is to seize or take hold of
on a film set this crew member handles and moves equipment

explanation.definitionFit: A firm hold is a seizing grasp, and a film technician who rigs cameras holds the same job title.

clue.text: Stand up with vase for Scottish artist

indicators.note: in a down clue, up reverses the word

parts.note: to stand something is to bear it
an urn is a vase

explanation.surface: Stand up holding a vase for a Scottish painter.
explanation.walkthrough: Henry Raeburn was a Scottish portrait painter.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Henry Raeburn was a Scottish portrait painter of the late eighteenth century.

clue.text: Stick last part of electoral roll in drawer

parts.note: paste is glue used to stick things

indicators.note: the last part of a word is its final letter

parts.note: a roll is a list of names

explanation.surface: Stick the final section of the electoral roll in a drawer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'drawer' is not furniture but someone who draws.
explanation.definitionFit: A pastellist is an artist who draws with pastels, so is a drawer.

clue.text: Female duo, perhaps, providing joint cover

parts.note: Pat is a woman's name, the first of a possible pair
Ella is another woman's name, completing the pair

explanation.surface: Two women team up to provide cover for a gathering.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'duo' is two women's names placed side by side; 'perhaps' warns that they are only examples.
explanation.definitionFit: The kneecap is the small bone covering the front of the knee joint.

clue.text: Wood or iron on the outskirts of Canterbury

indicators.note: the outskirts of a word are its first and last letters

parts.note: to iron clothes is to press them

explanation.surface: A forest or metal works found on the edge of a cathedral city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wood or iron' reads as a choice of materials, but 'or' merely links the definition to the wordplay. Canterbury is a cathedral city in Kent.
explanation.definitionFit: Cypress is a coniferous tree, and its timber is a named wood.

clue.text: Making ardent love on edge of cliff let down climber

parts.note: passion is ardent love

indicators.note: the edge of a word here is its final letter

parts.note: to lower is to let down

explanation.surface: Making passionate love at the edge of a cliff, a climber is let down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'climber' is a climbing plant, not a mountaineer.
explanation.definitionFit: The passionflower is a climbing plant, so it is a climber.

clue.text: Test skin wound with no difficulty

indicators.note: wound, as in twisted, tells us these letters are wound into a new order

explanation.surface: A skin test leaves a wound but causes no trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wound' looks like an injury but is the past tense of wind; 'with' just joins the two pieces of fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Something knotty is tangled and hard to solve, so this quality is complexity or difficulty.

clue.text: Truck in Oz reputed to be defective

indicators.note: defective means lacking parts, so only a fragment of the word is used

explanation.surface: An Australian lorry is said to be faulty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reputed' with its outer letters missing leaves the run inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: In Australian usage a ute is a utility vehicle, a small pickup truck.

clue.text: Expert, contracted out, had issue

indicators.note: out here means the contracted word lies outside the expert

parts.note: contracted means reduced
a pro is an expert

explanation.surface: An expert was taken out of the contract and caused trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'had issue' means had children, not had a problem.
explanation.definitionFit: To have issue is to bear offspring, which is to have reproduced.

clue.text: Book read from right to left by eastern flight controller

indicators.note: by means next to, so the two pieces sit side by side
reading from right to left turns the word book's synonym backwards

parts.note: a novel is a book

explanation.surface: Reading a book back to front, in the Eastern manner, beside a flight controller.
explanation.walkthrough: 'read from right to left' turns the synonym for Book backwards; 'by' sets the eastern letter beside it. Some scripts really are read that way, which suits the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: An elevon is an aircraft control surface that acts both as elevator and aileron, controlling flight.

clue.text: Local ordering ale or gin

indicators.note: ordering, as in arranging, rearranges these letters

explanation.surface: At the local pub, someone is ordering ale or gin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Local' suggests the pub where the drinks are ordered, but it is the adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: Regional and local both describe something belonging to a particular area.

clue.text: Part of the ordinary gains due for a change

indicators.note: for a change signals these letters are changed in order

explanation.surface: Ordinary gains are due for a change.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'ordinary' is the Ordinary of the Mass, its unvarying texts.
explanation.definitionFit: The Agnus Dei is one of the fixed sung parts of the Mass ordinary.

clue.text: Again take on top fruit

indicators.note: to top something is to cut off its head, so its first letter goes

parts.note: a greengage is a green variety of plum

explanation.surface: Hire again someone to pick fruit from the top of the tree.
explanation.walkthrough: 'top' is a verb: behead GREENGAGE, a kind of plum, removing its G.
explanation.definitionFit: To re-engage is to hire or employ once more.

clue.text: Set out with old hammer

parts.note: ex means former or old
to pound is to hammer

explanation.surface: Start with an old hammer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Set out' means explain, not depart.
explanation.definitionFit: To expound a theory is to set it out in detail.

clue.text: Tin god responsible for hidden dangers

parts.note: Sn is the chemical symbol for tin
Ares is the Greek god of war

explanation.surface: A tin idol is to blame for unseen perils.
explanation.walkthrough: 'responsible for' is only a link between wordplay and definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Traps are concealed devices to catch the unwary, so they are perils lying unseen.

clue.text: Asian capital formerly managed by board

parts.note: ran means managed
to board a vehicle is to go on it

explanation.surface: An Asian capital used to be managed by a board.
explanation.walkthrough: Rangoon, now Yangon, was formerly the capital of Burma; 'formerly' belongs to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Rangoon was the capital of Burma until 2006 and the city's older name.

clue.text: Fielding's eponymous heroine using a male writer's pseudonym

parts.note: Elia was the pen name of essayist Charles Lamb

explanation.surface: A heroine was named after a male writer's pen name.
explanation.walkthrough: Henry Fielding wrote the novel Amelia; Charles Lamb wrote the Essays of Elia.
explanation.definitionFit: Henry Fielding's 1751 novel is named after its heroine, Amelia Booth.

clue.text: Pickpocket may be lucky

definitions.meaning: in slang a ... is a thief who picks pockets
a lucky ... is a game where you draw an unseen prize from a tub

explanation.walkthrough: The second definition is a cryptic hint: the word can be preceded by 'lucky' in a common phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: Slang for a thief who lifts wallets, and the second half of a fairground lucky-prize game.

clue.text: Mineral out, mineral out

indicators.note: out signals that the letters are put out of order

explanation.surface: A repeated mineral is out of the running.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue repeats itself: the first 'Mineral' is the definition, then 'out, mineral' is anagram fodder and the final 'out' the signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Tourmaline is a crystalline boron silicate mineral, often cut as a gemstone.

clue.text: Head losing head on a single occasion

indicators.note: losing head means the first letter is dropped

parts.note: bonce is British slang for head

explanation.surface: A head was lost on one occasion.
explanation.walkthrough: BONCE is British slang for the head.
explanation.definitionFit: The adverb means one time only, on one occasion.

clue.text: Delighted as Conservative showed anger

parts.note: to huff is to show offended anger

explanation.surface: Pleased when a Tory lost their temper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'as' is a link word: the delight is defined as the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Chuffed is British slang for very pleased.

clue.text: Information from base

definitions.meaning: the inside facts or details about something
base meaning mean, contemptible or underhand

explanation.definitionFit: The inside story is informal for information, and a mean low trick is described with the same hyphenated word.

clue.text: It's extinct? Make two copies

indicators.note: two copies means the word is written twice

parts.note: to make something is to do it

explanation.surface: Is this creature dead? Then duplicate it.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark marks the definition as an example: one famous extinct bird.
explanation.definitionFit: The flightless bird of Mauritius died out in the 17th century and is the byword for extinction.

clue.text: Untidy island in Gide's novel

indicators.note: in puts the island inside the other letters
novel as an adjective means new, so the letters take a new form

parts.note: Arran is an island off western Scotland

explanation.surface: A messy island features in a book by André Gide.
explanation.walkthrough: 'novel' looks like Gide's book but is the anagram signal, and 'in' puts the Scottish island inside the rearranged letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To disarrange things is to put them in disorder, making them untidy; the definition is a verb.
